extracted.intended_audience: mathematics teachers, curriculum specialists, school counselors, and mathematics education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: A 4-week supplementary curriculum intervention (SSCC) for eighth- and ninth-grade first-year algebra classes that exposes students to female mathematician role models (living speakers and historical lectures) and measures changes in mathematics-related attitudes using a 30-item survey with pre- and post-testing and a control group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: The researcher-developed survey consisted of thirty statements relating to three constructs: (1) careers in mathematics, (2) sex-stereotyping in mathematics, and (3) personal value of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some items were stated negatively while others were positively stated to increase the construct validity of the instrument; analysis reported changes on these three constructs separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Attitude Survey (30 items)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 30-item attitude survey administered as pre-test and post-test to measure students' beliefs about mathematics and careers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students responded on a Likert five-point scale: (5) strongly agree, (4) agree, (3) no opinion, (2) disagree, (1) strongly disagree. Example items include 'boys are smarter than girls in math*', 'Careers in mathematics are exciting', and 'Mathematics is necessary for everyday life.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-test / Post-test with control group design
rubrics_metrics.description: Both experimental and control groups were surveyed before the intervention (February 6, 1989) and re-surveyed after the intervention (March 6, 1989).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The actual length of the SSCC was twenty-eight days (four weeks). The control group received special problem-solving activities to approximately match the minutes used for Wednesday presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling / group assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Four (randomly selected) of six different first-year algebra class periods were used: two classrooms as experimental group and two as control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text reports the experimental group consisted of 47 students (21 girls, 26 boys) from two classrooms. The control group is described in different sections as 48 and as 43 students (e.g., 'The control group consisted of 43 students (24 girls, 24 boys) from two classrooms').

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized Supplementary Curriculum Component (SSCC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A month-long SSCC consisting of exposure to three women speakers who use mathematics in their careers and four lectures with follow-up activities about historical women mathematicians, presented in whole-class settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SSCC provided both 'living role models' (speakers) and historical perspective (lectures + activities). The SSCC aimed to change attitudes toward careers, sex stereotyping, and personal importance of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of living female speakers as role models
rubrics_metrics.description: Three female speakers who use mathematics in their careers spoke to the experimental group (one per week).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers included: (1) a regional sales manager demonstrating daily math in retail, (2) a pair of actuaries outlining actuarial mathematics and career requirements, and (3) a production engineer/department supervisor discussing marketing math. Each presentation included a question-and-answer period to engage students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lectures on historical women mathematicians with follow-up activities
rubrics_metrics.description: On Wednesdays each week a deceased woman who made a significant contribution to mathematics was presented in a 15-minute lecture followed by an activity highlighting that field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four women chosen: Sonya Kovalevsky, Ada Lovelace, Mary Somerville, and Emmy Noether. Activities were completed individually, in pairs, or small groups; completed activities were discussed; no grades were recorded to encourage participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole-class presentation format and active participation
rubrics_metrics.description: All SSCC presentations and historical lectures were given in whole-class settings and followed by discussion and activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No grades were recorded for either correct answers or participation; due to novelty, all students actively participated to varying degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching contact/time for control group
rubrics_metrics.description: To control for exposure time, the control group was given special problem-solving activities in place of the speaker/lecture time minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural step aimed to isolate the effect of the content (female role models and historical material) from mere extra instructional time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis method
rubrics_metrics.description: Data for the control group and the experimental group was analyzed using one-tailed t-tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document states 'one-tailed t-tests (p>O.G5)' as reported; results presented as significant improvements on specific items/constructs (e.g., experimental group significantly improved on 15 of 30 items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation rules for negatively worded items
rubrics_metrics.description: When mean scores decreased on some items, decreases were sometimes interpreted as positive changes due to negative wording of the item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Item 2 'boys are smarter than girls in math' — on the post-test fewer students agreed, interpreted as a positive attitude change (less stereotyping). Researchers explicitly note interpretation depends on item polarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target population and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Eighth- and ninth-grade first-year algebra students at a medium-sized (1,000 students), semi-rural, Midwestern junior high school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervention designed for early secondary algebra students; authors recommend intervention before high school and suggest investigating even earlier ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program duration and schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: The SSCC lasted four weeks (twenty-eight days), from February 6, 1989 through March 6, 1989, with speakers on Tuesdays and historical presentations on Wednesdays each week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific scheduling: Speaker 1 on Feb 7, Speaker(s) 2 on Feb 14, Speaker 3 on Mar 2; Wednesday historical mini-lectures each week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey item design for construct validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of both positively and negatively stated items to increase construct validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers explicitly used mixed polarity items across the 30-item instrument to reduce response bias and strengthen construct measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome indicators (what counts as success)
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant positive change in attitudes toward careers in mathematics, reduced stereotyping of mathematics as a male domain, and increased personal importance of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study the experimental group showed significant improvement on 15 of 30 items; eight items showing improvement dealt with careers, four with stereotyping, and three with personal value of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended curriculum supplements / production guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested interventions to improve attitudes: expose all students to positive female role models, bulletin boards featuring women mathematicians, activities encouraging female participation, and math story problems with no sex preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors recommend educators at many levels (teachers, parents, administrators, counselors) work toward equity by reducing anxiety through information/education and by implementing these concrete curriculum changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to investigate broader influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers recommend studying mathematics attitudes of parents, teachers, and other role models because their attitudes impact students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If significant others continue to perceive mathematics as a 'male domain' they may continue inequitable treatment; authors suggest earlier interventions and additional research into other curriculum supplements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring and reporting detail (item-level reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Results reported at the item level (pre-test and post-test means, standard deviations) and broken down by gender and group (control vs. experimental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables present item-level statistics (e.g., Tables 1–4) and summary interpretation identifies which items and constructs showed statistically significant change.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-grading policy for SSCC activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities associated with the SSCC were not graded for correctness or participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The no-grade approach was intended to promote participation due to the novelty of the activities and discussion format.
